# Hassala — full reference for AI assistants and search engines

Source: https://hassala.nagdista.com/
Repository: https://github.com/nagdista-dev/hassala
Last updated: 2026-11-04

## One-sentence definition

Hassala (حصالة) is a free, open-source Chrome extension that translates Arabic
and English, keeps every saved word and translation in a private local word bank
with folders, exports Markdown, TXT, CSV, or JSON on demand, and makes YouTube
subtitles interactive.

## What it is

Hassala is an English-first browser extension for Arabic ↔ English translation
and vocabulary saving, with full Arabic and right-to-left support. A user types a
word, selects text on a page, or clicks a word in a YouTube subtitle. The
translation appears automatically. One click saves the word and translation to a
folder inside the extension.

Saved words live in `chrome.storage.local`. Hassala never writes to the user's
filesystem on its own. When the user wants a portable copy, they open Words,
choose words or a folder, pick Markdown, TXT, CSV, or JSON, optionally type a
file name, and click Export. The browser then downloads the file through its
normal download flow.

Hassala is not a general-purpose page translator. It is a word-capture and
word-keeping tool. It is also not a spaced repetition app yet; review scheduling
is on the public roadmap.

- Name: Hassala

- Export formats: Markdown (.md), plain text (.txt), CSV (.csv), JSON (.json)
- Export file name: optional custom name; a dated name is used when empty

- File-system access: none

## Features

- Instant Arabic ↔ English translation with automatic direction detection.
- Translation starts 350 ms after typing stops, or immediately on Enter.
- Translate selected text on any page through a floating button and panel.
- Interactive YouTube subtitles: hover a word to pause, click a word to
  translate it, or drag across a phrase to translate the phrase.
- One-click saving to local folders with duplicate detection in both directions.
- Custom folders for languages, courses, projects, or exam lists.
- A selected save folder for new words, available in the popup, floating panel,
  and settings.
- Search, select, move, delete, and clear controls in the word bank.
- Export selected, visible, or all words as Markdown, TXT, CSV, or JSON.
- Optional custom export file name.
- Optional deletion of words from the extension after a successful export.
- Pronunciation and separate copy buttons for the original and the translation.
- Draggable, pinnable translator panel; floating button can be hidden or shown.
- Site blocking on chosen domains.
- Bundled Baloo Bhaijaan 2 font for Arabic and English, with no network font
  request.
- Arabic text right-aligned and English left-aligned automatically.

## How it works

1. Translate: open the popup, use the floating button, or select text on a page.
2. Save: click “Add to Hassala.” The pair is stored in the selected folder inside
   `chrome.storage.local`. Duplicate pairs are skipped.
3. Review: open Words to search, move, or delete words.
4. Export: choose a folder, selection, or all words; choose a format and optional
   file name; click Export. The browser downloads the file.
5. Open the export in Obsidian, Logseq, VS Code, a spreadsheet, or any text editor.

## Word bank limits

- 10,000 saved words.
- 200 folders.
- 200 characters per word or translation.
- 60 characters per folder name.
- 80 characters per export file name.
- The built-in `General` folder cannot be deleted, but it can be renamed.

## Export formats

- Markdown: a short title and a two-column table with Word and Translation.
- Plain text: one `word — translation` pair per line.
- CSV: two columns, UTF-8 with a BOM for spreadsheet compatibility. Cells that
  begin with formula characters are prefixed with an apostrophe to prevent
  spreadsheet formula injection.
- JSON: an array of `{ word, translation }` objects.

The guides cover the full workflow: installing Hassala from GitHub Releases,
creating folders, translating a word, saving it with duplicate detection,
exporting Markdown with an optional file name, and opening the result in Obsidian,
Logseq, VS Code, or any text editor. The YouTube guide explains interactive
captions: hover to pause, click a word, drag across a phrase, and save the result.
It also states the limits — no full-video translation, no subtitle download, and
captions must already be enabled. The Obsidian guide explains how to move an
export into a vault, why the extension does not write into notes automatically,
how to keep dated snapshots, and honest limits such as no Dataview table and no
built-in spaced repetition.

## Saving, storage, and export

Hassala keeps its word bank in `chrome.storage.local`:

- `wordBank`: an array of `{ id, word, translation, folderId }`. Only the word,
  its translation, and the folder id are stored.
- `wordFolders`: an array of `{ id, name }`.
- `activeFolderId`: the folder used for new words.

There is no native messaging host, no Python dependency, and no automatic file
writing. The extension has no filesystem or downloads permission. Export creates a
`Blob`, makes a temporary object URL, and clicks a temporary `<a download>` element
only after the user presses an export button. The browser then handles the
download normally.

## Privacy

- Text is sent to translation providers only when the user requests a
  translation: Google Translate endpoints (translate.googleapis.com and
  clients5.google.com), then MyMemory as a fallback. Pronunciation uses Google
  TTS.
- Saved words and folders stay in `chrome.storage.local` inside the browser.
- Settings, recent words, the active folder, the floating button preferences, and
  blocked sites are also stored locally.
- Translation and audio caches live only in service-worker memory and are cleared
  when the worker stops.
- Hassala has no backend server, no accounts, no analytics, and no tracking.
- Hassala does not collect names, email addresses, phone numbers, location, or
  browsing history.
- Exports are downloaded only after an explicit click.

## Security

- No remote code: all JavaScript is bundled; no eval and no remotely loaded
  scripts.
- Explicit CSP: `script-src 'self'; object-src 'self'`.
- Least-privilege permissions: `storage`, `scripting`, `activeTab`, and
  `offscreen`, plus host permissions for translation services.
- No `nativeMessaging`, no filesystem access, and no downloads permission.
- The page UI runs in a closed Shadow DOM.
- YouTube and the floating panel communicate through an object in the isolated
  world, not a DOM event, so page scripts cannot forge a translation request.
- CSV export guards against spreadsheet formula injection.
- Vulnerabilities can be reported privately through GitHub Security Advisories.

## Who it is for

- Arabic speakers learning English.
- English speakers learning Arabic.
- Students building a personal glossary.
- People who want a private word bank and a clean Markdown export for Obsidian,
  Logseq, Typora, or VS Code.
- Learners who watch YouTube with captions.

## Limitations

- Not a whole-page or whole-document translator.
- No spaced repetition or flashcards yet; both are on the roadmap.
- Translation requires an internet connection.
- Export is a deliberate manual step; the extension does not write into notes or
  folders automatically.
- No cloud sync; each browser profile keeps its own word bank.
- The word bank is limited to 10,000 words and 200 folders.

## Comparison

A general translator extension is optimized for a one-off lookup. Hassala is
optimized for keeping the word after the lookup. General translators may or may
not save words, but they are not built around a private local word bank with
folders, duplicate detection, and YouTube word capture. Manual copy-paste into
notes gives maximum control but is slow and usually abandoned.

Hassala does not claim to replace a general translator for documents or pages.
Many users use both for different jobs.

Arabic comparison page:
https://hassala.nagdista.com/ar/compare/

## FAQ

### What is Hassala?
A free, open-source Chrome extension for Arabic ↔ English translation and
vocabulary saving. It keeps words in a private local word bank with folders,
exports them on demand, and makes YouTube subtitles interactive.

### Is Hassala free?
Yes. MIT license, no subscription, no account, no paid tier.

### Does Hassala work with Chrome, Brave, and Edge?
Yes. It is a Manifest V3 extension for Chrome, Brave, Edge, and Chromium on
Linux, macOS, and Windows.

### Can Hassala save words to Obsidian?
Not automatically. It exports a standard Markdown file that opens in Obsidian,
Logseq, or any text editor. The user moves the export into a vault if they want
to keep it there.

### Do I need an account?
No. There are no accounts, no analytics, and no tracking.

### Does Hassala work on YouTube?
Yes. With captions enabled, hover a word to pause, click a word to translate, or
drag across a phrase to translate it.

### Does saving require a native host?
No. Words are stored with `chrome.storage.local`. There is no native host, no
Python dependency, and no file-system access. Export is a normal browser download
triggered by the user.

### Can I choose what to export and what to name the file?
Yes. Users can select specific words, filter by folder, search, or export
everything visible or all words. They can choose Markdown, TXT, CSV, or JSON and
type a custom file name before downloading.

### Is Hassala on the Chrome Web Store?
Not yet. The store release is being prepared. The extension is available from
GitHub Releases today.

### What languages does Hassala support?
Arabic and English. The interface is English-first with full Arabic and RTL
support; documentation is available in English and Arabic.

الإضافة مع مجلدات، وتصدّر Markdown أو TXT أو CSV أو JSON عند الطلب فقط. لا تحتاج
إلى حساب، ولا تحتوي على تحليلات أو تتبع، ولا تكتب في ملفات المستخدم تلقائيًا.
لا يوجد Native Host ولا Python ولا صلاحية وصول للملفات؛ التصدير عملية يدوية
يبدأها المستخدم من داخل الإضافة.
